findings.description: AWS access key ID and secret access key are hard-coded in plaintext within the user_data script, which is stored in instance metadata, the EC2 console/API, and Terraform state, exposing long-lived AWS credentials to anyone with access to any of those.
The security group allows inbound TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing administrative access to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.
The security group allows inbound TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 with no compensating controls (e.g., WAF, TLS termination), exposing the web service to the entire internet in cleartext.

map_public_ip_on_launch is enabled, automatically assigning public IPs to any instance launched in this subnet; this subnet hosts the actual internet-facing web server, compounding exposure alongside the permissive security group.

map_public_ip_on_launch is enabled for this subnet, automatically assigning public IPs to any instance launched here even though no instance currently resides in it, unnecessarily expanding the network's potential public attack surface.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true (or a kms_key_id), so data written to disk by the internet-facing web server is stored unencrypted, violating encryption-at-rest requirements.

The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration), leaving potentially sensitive network traffic metadata unencrypted at rest.

The S3 bucket has no public access block, bucket policy, or ACL restrictions defined, leaving it reliant on account defaults and susceptible to misconfiguration-driven public exposure of flow log data.
